Monday: Mahima waited after the bell and asked Pooja Ma'am, the class teacher, "Is there any way to reduce the fees? Papa's shop has been slow this year." Pooja Ma'am did not look surprised. "There are concessions and a scholarship form. The deadline is the 28th. Bring the income paper and last year's marksheet."

Thursday: At home Mahima and Mummy laid the papers on the bed: income certificate, marksheet, a copy of the ration card, two photos. One document was missing, and Papa said he would fetch it from the office on Saturday.

The 26th: Mahima handed the completed form to Pooja Ma'am, who ticked a checklist. "Two days early," she said. The result would take weeks, but Mahima walked home lighter.

qa.q: What was the deadline for the scholarship form?
How did Mahima feel after handing in the form?
qa.a: Mahima felt lighter and relieved, because the form was in early and the worry was now in formal hands.

qa.q: What else could Mahima do while waiting for the result, and why?
qa.a: Mahima could ask Pooja Ma'am whether another school support scheme exists, because more than one formal option may help.

qa.q: How does Pooja Ma'am see Mahima's question?
qa.a: Pooja Ma'am did not look surprised, so this is a familiar situation, and a student who asks early and brings the documents is easy to help.

grounding: The teen asks the class teacher about fee concessions and scholarships, gathers documents with parents, and applies before the deadline, using formal help that exists for such situations.

passage: Harish kanna, you think asking for help is shameful? Let your Lakshmi Paati tell you something. When I was fifteen, my father's mill closed, and I thought I'd have to leave school. I cried for two days. Then I went to my class teacher, Miss Rosamma, after the bell and asked straight out: is there any help for girls whose families can't pay? She told me about the fee concession and a state scholarship, and that the forms were due in three weeks. My father and I spent two evenings at the taluk office getting the income certificate. I copied my mark sheets out neatly by hand. We handed it all in five days early. I got both. That is how your Paati finished school, kanna. The help existed. I only had to ask for it.

qa.q: How did young Lakshmi feel when the mill closed?
qa.a: She was frightened and upset, crying for two days, thinking she would have to leave school.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made the difference?
qa.a: Asking Miss Rosamma directly about help, which led to the concession and scholarship, then gathering documents with her father and applying early.

qa.q: How might young Lakshmi's father have felt at the taluk office?
qa.a: He may have felt relieved and proud that his daughter had found a way, and glad to help with the certificate.

grounding: An elder recalls asking her class teacher about fee concessions and scholarships, gathering documents with her father and applying early.

passage: Trisha found out about the merit-cum-means scholarship on a Monday, from a notice half-hidden behind the sports timetable. The deadline was Friday. Her father was away driving a truck to Nagpur until Sunday, and the income certificate was somewhere in his files. At lunch she went to Pallavi Ma'am, her class teacher. "Ma'am, can I apply? Papa's work has been less since the summer." Pallavi Ma'am read the notice, then wrote out a checklist: mark sheet, income certificate, ID proof, bank details. "The fee concession forms are in the office too. Take both." That evening Trisha and her mother emptied the steel trunk of files onto the floor and found everything but the certificate. Her mother phoned Papa, who told them which folder. On Thursday afternoon, a day early, Trisha handed in both forms, every line of the checklist ticked.

qa.q: How might Trisha have felt when she saw the Friday deadline?
qa.a: She probably felt anxious and rushed, with Papa away and the certificate lost somewhere in his files.

qa.q: What helped Trisha meet the deadline?
qa.a: Asking Pallavi Ma'am quickly, following her checklist, and going through the documents with her mother, calling Papa for the missing folder.

qa.q: How does Pallavi Ma'am respond to Trisha's question?
qa.a: She takes it seriously and practically, writing a checklist and pointing Trisha to the fee concession forms as well.

grounding: Shows a teen asking her class teacher about scholarships and fee concessions, gathering documents with her mother and applying before the deadline.
